 IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF OHIO
 ELEVENTH APPELLATE DISTRICT
 LAKE COUNTY

NANCI ACOSTA, et al., CASE NO. 2026-L-0006

 Plaintiffs-Appellants,
 Civil Appeal from the
 - vs - Court of Common Pleas

TANIA RUBALCAVA, et al.,
 Trial Court No. 2023 CV 000790
 Defendants-Appellees.

 OPINION AND JUDGMENT ENTRY

 Decided: October 13, 2026
 Judgment: Affirmed

Erik L. Walter, Dworken & Bernstein Co., L.P.A., 60 South Park Place, Painesville, OH
44077 (For Plaintiffs-Appellants).

Matthew Vincel, Michael E. Hamper, III, and Zoe M. Suntheimer, The Legal Aid Society
of Cleveland, 1223 West Sixth Street, Cleveland, OH 44113 (For Defendants-
Appellees).

EUGENE A. LUCCI, J.

 {¶1} Appellants, Nanci Acosta, et al., appeal from the final judgment of the Lake

County Court of Common Pleas, after a trial to the bench, concluding that the contract

into which appellants and appellees, Tania Rubalcava, et al.,1 entered was a land

installment contract rather than a lease agreement with the option to purchase certain

1. We point out that, although the underlying complaint and this court’s case management system indicates
appellee Tania’s last name is “Rubalcava,” during her direct examination she spelled her name for the
record. Specifically, Tania stated “[m]y name is Tania . . . R as in Robert, U as in umbrella V as in Victor, A
as in Adam, C as in Charlie, A as in apple, L as in Larry, V as in Victor, A as in apple.” Accordingly, Tania
testified her last name is “Ruvacalva.” Because, however, the court filings regularly refer to Tania’s last
name as “Rubalcava,” this court’s opinion shall use that name, even though it would appear, given Tania’s
testimony, her true last name is Ruvacalva.
 residential property. At issue is whether the trial court’s legal determination was against

the manifest weight of the evidence. We affirm the trial court’s decision.

 I. Facts and Procedural History

 {¶2} Ms. Acosta and Ms. Rubalcava are sisters-in-law. Their husbands are

brothers and Ms. Acosta, with her husband, owned, at the time of the transaction at issue,

the underlying real estate which formed the basis of the contract at issue.

 {¶3} On September 14, 2019, appellants and appellees entered into an

“Agreement to Sell Real Estate” (“Sales Agreement”) located at 146 Linden Drive,

Painesville Township, Ohio 44077. The Sales Agreement provided, at paragraph 2(a),

that the property’s purchase price is “$105,000.00” and that appellees would pay a

“[d]eposit” of “$15,000.00[.]” Paragraph 2(c) of the contract additionally stated that a

$1,000 “monthly payment” would be “due the 1st[,]” presumably of each month. The same

paragraph additionally provided, however, that $90,000 “[c]ash, or certified or local

cashier’s check, due on closing and delivery of deed (or such greater or lesser amount

as may be necessary to complete payment of purchase price after credits, adjustments[,]

and prorations.” And, at paragraph 19, the Sales Agreement provided that the “contract

shall be closed and the deed and possession shall be delivered on or before” November

1, 2019, “unless extended by other provisions of this contract.”

 {¶4} Shortly after the contract was signed, Ms. Rubalcava testified that Ms.

Acosta expressly stated that the $1,000 monthly payment would be deducted from the

$90,000 owed. Ms. Rubalcava stated this representation occurred only “minutes” after

the contract was signed. Ms. Rubalcava asserted that this was the collective

understanding of the parties at the time of contract, and appellants did not challenge this

Case No. 2026-L-0006
 understanding. Moreover, during a follow-up conversation, Ms. Rubalcava testified that

Ms. Acosta represented that appellees would have five years to pay the $90,000 balance

(despite the language in paragraph 19).

 {¶5} Given Ms. Acosta’s alleged statement, Ms. Rubalcava understood she

would have paid $60,000 ($12,000 X 5 years) against the outstanding $90,000 owed and,

thus, would owe and be required to pay $30,000 before or at the end of the five-year

period.

 {¶6} Appellees paid the $15,000 “deposit,” and appellants placed the funds into

their personal account. Appellees moved into the residence on November 1, 2019. At that

point, appellees commenced payments of $1,000 per month.

 {¶7} In February 2022, Ms. Rubalcava received a letter from Ms. Acosta which

read:

 This letter is a notice to review our agreement signed on
 November 1, 2019 for the rent to buy property located at 146
 Linden dr. It was agreed by both parties that Monthly
 payments in the amount of $1,000 would be made to the
 owner of the property along with lump sum amounts to be able
 to reach the 5-year mark agreed upon to have the property
 paid off in full and or acquire a loan by a bank of your choice
 to have the property paid in full as stated in the Sale
 agreement signed on Nov 1. At this point you have breached
 your contract due to failure to pay lump sum amounts. Below
 are two options I will offer in regards to this matter.

 A: Return the property and treat your monthly payments as
 rent.

 B: Acquire a loan in the remaining amount of the sale to pay
 off property within 6 months.

(Sic. throughout.)
 {¶8} Ms. Rubalcava disputed that an arrangement was reached between the

parties for appellees to pay any “lump sum” amount prior to the expiration of the five-year

 PAGE 3 OF 26

Case No. 2026-L-0006
 term. Further, Ms. Rubalcava stated appellees did not fail to make the $1,000 payments

as set forth in the agreement. And pursuant to the post-agreement discussions, she

believed she had five years before any final sum would be due.

 {¶9} At trial, Ms. Acosta claimed that appellees failed to make certain payments

on the real estate. In her deposition testimony, however, Ms. Acosta stated appellees did

not miss a payment and continued to make payments on the property taxes when they

were due. Appellees’ counsel impeached Ms. Acosta’s testimony with her deposition

testimony at trial. Ms. Acosta was not able to reconcile the inconsistencies.

 {¶10} Further, Ms. Acosta testified at trial that the parties met in February 2021

to discuss the contract. During her deposition, however, Ms. Acosta stated the parties

met around “March 2022.” During the meeting, Ms. Acosta stated she agreed to give

appellees until January 2023 to pay the full amount.

 {¶11} Despite the various communications and Ms. Acosta’s alleged verbal and

acknowledged written representations regarding the five-year window,2 appellants filed

their complaint for forcible entry and detainer and for rent/damages against appellees on

October 7, 2022, in the Painesville Municipal Court. Appellees filed an answer and

counterclaims. In the initial counterclaim, appellees sought declaratory judgment that a

land installment contract was legitimately formed by the parties; appellees also claimed

appellants engaged in fraud, and that their complaint, if successful, would result in unjust

enrichment. In the second and third counterclaims, appellees sought damages that

2023 was the timeframe to which she agreed. This testimony is arithmetically inaccurate. If, as her letter
and Ms. Rubalcava’s testimony reflect, the window for final payment was five years from the entry of the
agreement, final payment would be due on September 14, 2024.

 amounted to a total of $175,000, an amount that exceeded the monetary jurisdiction of

the municipal court.

 {¶12} Appellees moved the municipal court to transfer the entirety of the matter to

the court of common pleas. On November 4, 2022, the municipal court issued a judgment

ordering the matter certified to the Lake County Court of Common Pleas. The municipal

court, however, did not remove the matter and the scheduled hearing date of November

10 remained apparently in effect.

 {¶13} Because the matter was not removed from the municipal court docket,

appellees filed a motion for clarification of the November 4, 2022 judgment. Appellants

filed a brief in opposition to appellees’ motion to transfer. On November 10, 2022, the

municipal court issued a judgment entry purporting to “void” its November 4, 2022 transfer

order. The court then granted appellants until November 21, 2022, to file a motion to

dismiss appellees’ counterclaims and afforded appellants until November 28, 2022, to

respond.

 {¶14} Appellants filed their motion to dismiss, and appellees duly opposed the

motion. The motion was not formally ruled upon. The municipal court, however, on

December 6, 2022, granted appellants’ complaint for forcible entry and detainer and

ordered appellants’ restitution of the premises. The municipal court indicated in the

judgment entry that appellants’ count alleging money damages remained pending. Upon

appellees’ motion, the municipal court stayed the judgment pending appeal.

 {¶15} Appellees appealed the decision to this court.

 {¶16} In Acosta v. Rubalcava, 2023-Ohio-1794 (11th Dist.), this court reversed

and remanded the matter. This court first determined “that the forcible entry and detainer

 PAGE 5 OF 26

Case No. 2026-L-0006
 action and the counterclaim are so interrelated that they could not be decided separately.”

Id. at ¶ 13. As such, this court held “in light of the interrelationship of the claims and

because the counterclaim requested damages were in excess $15,000, the municipal

court did not have jurisdiction over this action.” Id. at ¶ 14. This court consequently

ordered the matter to be transferred to the court of common pleas. Id. at ¶ 27. This court

further observed that, because appellees did not have an opportunity to present evidence

or be heard before the trial court granted appellants’ complaint, appellees’ right to due

process was violated. Id. at ¶ 23, 26-27.

 {¶17} Upon remand, the matter proceeded to a bench trial in the Lake County

Court of Common Pleas. After hearing evidence, the trial court, on December 29, 2025,

concluded the September 14, 2019 Sales Agreement between the parties was an

enforceable land installment contract. Specifically, the trial court cited R.C. 5313.02(A)

which sets forth 16 provisions that a contract must include in order for it to be deemed a

land installment contract. The trial court, however, noted that this court has determined

that regardless of the mandatory language of R.C. 5313.02, a land installment contract

may be enforceable even without strict compliance. See Phillips v. May, 2004-Ohio-5942,

¶ 21 (11th Dist.). The trial court further concluded, in light of the contractual language, the

agreement was ambiguous and it was therefore permitted to consider extrinsic evidence.

After reviewing the contract, the trial court concluded the contract was legally sufficient to

meet the requirements of law thereby creating a valid land installment contract.

 {¶18} The court additionally concluded that even if the contract were a rental

agreement, appellants would not be entitled to restitution because they accepted future

alleged rent payments after posting notices to vacate.

 PAGE 6 OF 26

Case No. 2026-L-0006
  {¶19} The trial court accordingly concluded appellees were entitled to declaratory

judgment on their claim that the Sales Agreement at issue was a land installment contract.

The trial court determined appellees’ claims for fraud and unjust enrichment were moot.

By implication, appellants’ claims against appellees were denied. This appeal follows.

 {¶20} Appellants assign the following as error:

 {¶21} “The trial court erred in finding that the agreement between the parties was

a land contract.”

 II. Standard of Review

 {¶22} Appellants essentially assert a manifest-weight-of-the-evidence challenge.

 {¶23} This court has observed that, in an “‘ap

Iken v Bohemian Brethren Presbyt. Church 
 2026 NY Slip Op 05909 
 October 13, 2026 
 Appellate Division, First Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Monica Iken, et al., Plaintiffs-Respondents, 
 v 
 Bohemian Brethren Presbyterian Church, Defendant-Appellant. 

 Decided and Entered: October 13, 2026 
 Index No. 654614/17|Appeal No. 7216-7216A,7216B,7216C,7216D|Case No. 2025-05827| 
 Before: Moulton, J.P., Scarpulla, Michael, Hagler, JJ. 

 McLaughlin & Stern, LLP, New York (Charles F. Kellett of counsel), for appellant. 
 Law Offices of Jonathan E. Neuman, Fresh Meadows (Jonathan E. Neuman of counsel), for respondents. 

 [*1] 
 Judgment, Supreme Court, New York County (Joel M. Cohen, J.), entered August 20, 2025, after a jury trial, awarding plaintiffs Monica Iken and Ordinary Faces LLC the amount of $1,216,177.36, and bringing up for review (1) an order, same court and Justice, entered on or about May 16, 2025, which denied the landlord's motion under CPLR 4404 to set aside the verdict; (2) an order, same court and Justice, entered on or about November 12, 2024, which denied defendant's motion to strike plaintiffs' jury demand; (3) an order, same court and Justice, entered on or about December 3, 2024, to the extent the order denied renewal of defendant's motion to strike the jury waiver; and (4) an order, same court and Justice, entered on or about December 19, 2024, which denied defendant's motion in limine to preclude Iken from testifying about her status as a 9/11 widow, unanimously affirmed, without costs. 
 "A determination that a verdict was based on legally insufficient evidence requires a finding that there is simply no valid line of reasoning and permissible inferences which could possibly lead rational [people] to the conclusion reached by the jury on the basis of the evidence presented at trial" ( Rivera v 4064 Realty Co. , 17 AD3d 201, 202-203 [1st Dept 2005], lv denied 5 NY3d 713 [2005] [internal quotation marks omitted]). Defendant failed to satisfy this heavy burden. The evidence adduced from plaintiffs' testimony and the parties' joint trial exhibits established that defendant breached its duties (1) under section 18(a) of the parties' lease to cooperate with plaintiffs to obtain the necessary approvals for the operation of the preschool by failing to file the paperwork necessary to clear violations issued by the New York City Department of Buildings (DOB) related to a defunct dumbwaiter shaft, and (2) under the lease rider to act "expeditiously and diligently" to assist plaintiffs with the installation of a fire alarm system. 
 The undisputed evidence at trial showed that the lack of a functional fire alarm system was the reason DOB denied plaintiff's initial application for a letter of no objection (LNO) needed to operate a preschool. Further, the FDNY did not sign off on the fire alarm system until July 26, 2016, nearly two years after the lease was signed. The evidence also supported plaintiffs' assertion that the DOB violations relating to the elevator prevented plaintiffs from obtaining the LNO. Considering that the violations were issued against portions of the building that were not included in the demised premises, it was defendant's obligation to cure them. 
 [*2] 
 Defendant's argument that there is no evidence that plaintiffs were unable to obtain the necessary LNO because of the violations is refuted by the joint trial exhibits and trial testimony. The DOB training module submitted as a joint trial exhibit expressly states that an LNO request generally will be denied if there are active violations, which Iken testified was the only remaining obstacle to obtaining a permanent LNO for the preschool. For its part, defendant failed to present evidence that plaintiffs could have obtained an LNO that would run for the duration of the preschool's two-year license period while the violations remained uncured. Indeed, defendant's treasurer and church elder, Deborah Ann Widerkehr, testified that defendant never complied with plaintiffs' request to have its elevator company file the paperwork necessary to clear the violation. Aside from the two letters defendant wrote to the DOB stating that there was no elevator in the building and asking that the violations be cleared, there is no evidence that defendant took any other steps to cure the violations, establishing their breach of section 18(a). 
 Defendant's assertion that the sole remedy under the lease rider for any delay was the 50% rent abatement from January through August 2015 that plaintiffs received is unavailing. Nothing in the rider's provision that both parties were required to "act expeditiously and diligently to obtain the proper permits, commence the work necessary to install the proper fire alarm system and obtain inspections and sign-offs" stated that the abatement was the exclusive remedy if defendant continued to fail to cooperate in plaintiffs' efforts to secure the fire alarm system ( see Biotronik A.G. v Conor Medsystems Ireland, Ltd. , 22 NY3d 799, 805 [2014] [rejecting argument that lost profits were unavailable because "[t]he limitations provision does not specifically preclude recovery for lost profits"]). 
 Defendant's challenge to the jury's lost profit award is also unavailing. Plaintiffs submitted competent evidence showing that that (1) "the damages [were] caused by the breach, (2) the extent of the loss is capable of proof with reasonable certainty, and (3) . . . the damages were fairly within the contemplation of the parties" ( id. at 806 [internal quotation marks omitted]). Specifically, the joint exhibits and testimony established that (1) plaintiffs were unable to operate the preschool as a direct result of the landlord's breaches of the lease and rider; (2) the losses were calculable based on data from a preschool that had previously operated in the same location for nearly 40 years and the tenant's first-year profits corresponded to the projections; and (3) the profits were within the parties' contemplation based on plaintiffs' business plan, prepared at defendant's request. 
 [*3] 
 Defendant's contention that the claimed lost profits were not supported by expert testimony or that Iken failed to lay a foundation for profits generated by the preschool that previously occupied the premises ignores Iken's testimony that defendant itself provided those operating figures to her, a fact which could have persuaded the jury that the numbers were acceptable to defendant. Plaintiffs observe that the award of $734,353 approximates 2.5 years of anticipated profits based on the projections in the joint trial exhibit. Thus, plaintiffs' lost profits were estimated "with the requisite degree of reasonable certainty" ( Kenford Co. v County of Erie , 67 NY2d 257, 261 [1986]). Significantly, defendant failed to present any countervailing evidence to show that plaintiffs' 2016 profits were an aberration or any other evidence with respect to lost profits that would render these figures speculative. 
 Section 19 of the lease, which provided that "Tenant shall look only and solely to Landlord's estate and interest in and to the Building and the rents and profits therefrom for the satisfaction of any right of Tenant arising out of this Lease or for the collection of judgment," and no other "property or assets" of defendant, did not preclude a damages award for plaintiffs after defendant's sale of the building. Similar clauses have been interpreted to permit parties to pursue real property sales proceeds, which reflect the seller's equity in the property ( see City of New York v Evanston Ins. Co. , 165 AD3d 1032, 1035 [2d Dept 2018]; Won's Cards v Samsondale/Haverstraw Equities, 165 AD2d 157, 164 [3d Dept 1991]). Defendant presented no evidence that the jury award exceeds its profits from the 2019 sale. 
 Defendant's motion to strike the jury demand was properly rejected. The jury waivers in the lease were raised for the first time four months after plaintiffs filed their note of issue, and well after defendant's counsel had represented on the record that there was "[n]o disagreement about the right to a jury trial." Under the circumstances, the court reasonably determined that the jury waiver had been waived ( see e.g. Sapp v Propeller Co. LLC , 12 AD3d 218, 219 [1st Dept 2004]). 
 Finally, there is no basis to set aside the verdict or to direct a new trial based on Iken's testimony relating to her husband's death in the September 11, 2001 attacks. Defendant acknowledges that none of the questions posed by plaintiffs' counsel directly mentioned his death, and the brief, unsolicited testimony was directly related to how she came to obtain the donated fire alarm system. Further, although defendant made a motion in limine to exclude this testimony, its counsel did not object at trial. In any event, given the weight of evidence supporting the verdict, the "isolated" statements were "not the type of comments that could have deprived defendant of a fair trial" ( Nieves v Riverbay Corp. , 95 AD3d 458, 459 [1st Dept 2012]). 
 [*4] 
 We have considered defendant's remaining contentions and find them unavailing. 
 THIS CONSTITUTES THE DECISION AND ORDER OF THE SUPREME COURT, APPELLATE DIVISION, FIRST DEPARTMENT. 
 ENTERED: October 13, 2026

 In the Matter of Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., Plaintiff-Respondent, 
 v 
 George Papailias, Defendant-Appellant, Giulia Papailias et al., Defendants-Respondents. 

 Decided and Entered: October 13, 2026 
 Index No. 850305/24|Appeal No. 7222|Case No. 2025-07806| 
 Before: Moulton, J.P., Scarpulla, Michael, Hagler, JJ. 

 The Kearney Law Group, New York (Cannon C. Kearney of counsel), for appellant. 
 Reed Smith LLP, New York (Ofunne N. Edoziem of counsel), for Giulia Papailias, respondent. 

 [*1] 
 Order, Supreme Court, New York County (Francis A. Kahn, III, J.), entered on or about November 17, 2025, which, to the extent appealed, granted plaintiff's motion for summary judgment on its mortgage foreclosure claim and appointed a referee to compute, and dismissed defendant George Papailias's affirmative defenses, unanimously affirmed, without costs. 
 Plaintiff adequately established defendant George Papailias's default. Plaintiff's submissions established that plaintiff itself made the records concerning the default, not a third party. Jaci Stevens, plaintiff's vice president of loan documentation, submitted an affidavit, based on her personal knowledge, which established that the records showing defendant's default were admissible as business records because they were made in the regular course of plaintiff's business and the relevant records were made at or near the time of the occurrences they reflected, by persons with personal knowledge of the matters contained therein or from information transmitted by people with such personal knowledge ( see CPLR 4518[a]). 
 Plaintiff also established that it complied with RPAPL 1304. Stevens attested to familiarity with the mailing practices of nonparty COVIUS Holdings LLC, plaintiff's agent responsible for the mailings. She provided detailed information concerning how mailing records were maintained, transmitted, and incorporated into plaintiff's mortgage files and business records, and how plaintiff routinely relied upon them in the course of its business. She also included copies of the records, which contained information documenting the mailing procedures. Stevens' testimony and the accompanying records satisfied plaintiff's prima facie burden of establishing that plaintiff sent the required statutory notices ( see Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Gordon , 171 AD3d 197 , 209 [2d Dept 2019]). Defendant's sworn denial of receipt did not, standing alone, raise a question of fact as to non-delivery ( see CIT Bank N.A. v Schiffman , 36 NY3d 550 , 557 [2021]). 
 Plaintiff established its standing by attaching a copy of the note, endorsed to plaintiff, to the complaint ( see Bank of N.Y. Mellon Trust Co. N.A ., 95 AD3d 695 [1st Dept 2012]; see also JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. v Grennan , 175 AD3d 1513 , 1516 [2d Dept 2019]). In any event, plaintiff also established that it possessed the note in 2024, when it brought this action, by including records showing that plaintiff retained possession of the note at the time the complaint was filed and by attesting that these and other documents plaintiff made were business records. 
 [*2] 
 We have considered and rejected defendant's arguments concerning the court's failure to address dismissal of each affirmative defense individually, because the record is sufficient for us to review the viability of the defenses ( see Matter of Horowitz v Zucker , 172 AD3d 538 , 539 [1st Dept 2019], lv denied 33 NY3d 913 [2019]). Upon such review, we conclude that the defenses were properly dismissed as either refuted by plaintiff's proof or because they were otherwise conclusory and unsupported by any facts in the answer or in opposition to plaintiff's summary judgment motion. To the extent defendant failed to address certain of the affirmative defenses in opposition to plaintiff's summary judgment motion, those defenses are deemed abandoned. 
 THIS CONSTITUTES THE DECISION AND ORDER OF THE SUPREME COURT, APPELLATE DIVISION, FIRST DEPARTMENT. 
 ENTERED: October 13, 2026

Kenworthy, Judge. 
Case Summary 
[1] This interlocutory appeal concerns eleven passenger vans owned by Model 1 
Commercial Vehicles, Inc. (“Model 1”) currently in the possession of Reindeer 
Logistics, LLC (“Reindeer”) and held in storage facilities outside of Indiana. 
Model 1 brought an action to replevy the vans, which Reindeer claimed to be 
holding as security for a debt. The trial court granted Model 1 a preliminary 
order for immediate possession under the Indiana replevin statute, contingent 
on Model 1 posting a $1.1 million bond. 
[2] Reindeer appealed, and Model 1 moved to dismiss, arguing the interlocutory 
order is not appealable as of right. We hold we do not have jurisdiction to 
review the trial court’s preliminary possession order under the facts and 
circumstances of this case. Accordingly, we dismiss the appeal. 
Facts and Procedural History 
[3] Model 1 sells, leases, and finances the purchase of commercial vehicles such as 
vans, buses, and work trucks. Los Angeles-based Zeeba Automotive Group, 
Inc. (“Zeeba”) rents commercial vehicles to customers across the United States. 
To carry out its rental business, Zeeba sometimes contracts with companies like 
Reindeer, which provides vehicle moving and storage services throughout the 
country. 
Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 25A-CE-2496 | October 13, 2026 Page 3 of 12 

[4] In 2024, under several separate agreements, Model 1 leased Zeeba a total of 
sixty-eight Ford passenger vans for use in Zeeba’s rental business. Zeeba 
intended to purchase the vans from Model 1, but after Zeeba’s financing fell 
through, the parties renegotiated the contracts and entered into a single, 
superseding master lease agreement for sixty-two of the vans (the “master 
lease”). Under the master lease terms, Model 1 retained ownership of the vans, 
and Zeeba had a possessory right to use and operate them. 
[5] Soon after executing the master lease, Zeeba defaulted on its payment 
obligations. After some negotiation and attempts to resolve the matter, Model 
1 sent Zeeba a letter on May 9, 2025, terminating the master lease for 
nonpayment. Model 1 also demanded return of all the vans. 
[6] Not all vans, however, were in Zeeba’s possession and available to be returned. 
Some were leased to Zeeba’s customers, others were stored by vehicle 
transportation companies like Reindeer, and some were even unaccounted for. 
Relevant to this appeal, Zeeba informed Model 1 that eleven vans were in 
Reindeer’s possession and stored in Reindeer facilities in California, 
Massachusetts, and Tennessee. Zeeba advised Model 1 to work directly with 
Reindeer to “get those vehicles released,” essentially because Zeeba did not 
have the revenue to pay Reindeer for services rendered. Ex. Vol. 1 at 24. Model 
1 contacted Reindeer, but Reindeer refused to turn over the vans; Reindeer was 
retaining possession due to Zeeba’s outstanding debt. 
Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 25A-CE-2496 | October 13, 2026 Page 4 of 12 

[7] On August 8, 2025, Model 1 brought a complaint for replevin, breach of lease, 
and damages against Zeeba. It also named as defendants Reindeer and another 
vehicle transportation company called Total Auto Movers, Inc. (“TAM”). 1 
Model 1 contemporaneously moved for a preliminary order for immediate 
possession of all vans the defendants held. The trial court issued an order to 
show cause and scheduled a hearing for August 25, 2025. 
[8] Reindeer filed a response in opposition to Model 1’s motion. Reindeer did not 
dispute Model 1 owned the eleven vans Reindeer currently held. But Reindeer 
argued it came into possession of the vans legally pursuant to a contract with 
Zeeba and asserted a “valid possessory lien” for $62,604 in unpaid storage, 
transport, and other charges incurred by Zeeba related to those eleven vehicles. 
Appellant’s App. Vol. 2 at 63. Reindeer claimed it was lawfully entitled to detain 
the vans until its charges were paid or adequate security was posted.
2 In 
support of its response, Reindeer attached an affidavit of its corporate executive, 
a copy of its agreement with Zeeba, and a list of unpaid charges related to the 
eleven vans. 
[9] The trial court held a hearing, after which Zeeba began working with Model 1 
to return some of the vans to which it had access. Reindeer did not return the 

1 Like Reindeer, TAM transports motor vehicles and possesses Model 1 vans via a contract with Zeeba. 
Neither Zeeba nor TAM is party to this appeal. 
2 Reindeer also argued the trial court did not have in rem jurisdiction over vans located outside Indiana and 
therefore had no authority to order the county sheriff or officials in out-of-state jurisdictions to seize them. 
See id. at 64–65.

eleven vans it held. On September 24, 2025, the trial court entered findings and 
granted Model 1 a preliminary order for immediate possession of the 
unreturned vans, effective once Model 1 posted a written undertaking of $1.1 
million (representing the estimated value of all the unreturned vans). It further 
ordered that upon Model 1’s posting of the written undertaking, “Reindeer is 
directed to immediately deliver the Model 1 Vans to Model 1 unless Reindeer 
files with the Court a written undertaking in the amount of $605,000 [the 
estimated value of the eleven vans in Reindeer’s possession].” Id. at 16. Two 
days later, Model 1 posted the replevin bond; Reindeer did not file a written 
undertaking to stay delivery of the vans. 
[10] Reindeer moved the trial court to certify the order for discretionary 
interlocutory appeal and to stay its execution. At the same time, Reindeer filed 
its notice of appeal with this Court, designating the appeal as one taken from an 
interlocutory order as of right. The trial court denied Reindeer’s motion to 
certify and stay the order. In this Court, Model 1 moved to dismiss Reindeer’s 
appeal, arguing the order for possession does not fall into any category which 
would entitle Reindeer to an interlocutory appeal. After Reindeer responded, 
this Court’s motions panel issued an order holding the motion to dismiss in 
abeyance for the writing panel to address. 
Reindeer is not entitled to an interlocutory appeal. 
[11] We review appellate jurisdictional questions de novo. Ball State Univ. v. Irons, 27 
N.E.3d 717, 720 (Ind. 2015). The appellate authority of this Court is generally 
limited to appeals from final judgments. Id. A preliminary order for immediate

possession, such as the one issued in this case, is not a final judgment. See Ind. 
Code § 32-35-2-15 (2002) (authorizing a prejudgment order for possession under 
replevin statute); I.C. § 32-35-2-20 (differentiating an order for possession and 
other preliminary orders in a replevin action from a final judgment). 
[12] But our Rules of Appellate Procedure also confer appellate jurisdiction over 
certain non-final orders under Indiana Appellate Rule 14. Irons, 27 N.E.3d at 
720. “There are three ways a case may proceed as an interlocutory appeal: an

(Rule 14(B)); or an interlocutory appeal from an order granting or denying

immediate possession order for discretionary interlocutory appeal and the class-

if the order qualifies as at least one of the nine order types which entitle a party 
to an interlocutory appeal of right. See Ind. Appellate Rule 14(A)(1)–(9). 
[13] Reindeer contends its appeal is proper under Rule 14(A)(3), which entitles a 
party to appeal an interlocutory order to “compel the delivery or assignment of

14(A)(3). The list is non-exclusive; as the Indiana Supreme Court has 
explained, Rule 14(A)(3) encompasses court orders “which carry financial and

27 N.E.3d at 721 (quoting State v. Hogan, 582 N.E.2d 824, 825 (Ind. 1991)). 
Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 25A-CE-2496 | October 13, 2026 Page 7 of 12 

The rule is not, however, “designed to create an appeal as of right from every

[14] In support of its argument that it is entitled to an interlocutory appeal, Reindeer 
relies on Ball State University v. Irons, 27 N.E.3d 717 (Ind. 2015). That case arose

attended Ball State University but wanted to transfer to another school. The

 JUSTICE COBBS delivered the judgment of the court.
 Presiding Justice Ellis and Justice Fitzgerald Smith concurred in the judgment.

 ORDER

¶1 Held: We affirm the circuit court’s eviction order where defendant presented no defenses
 germane to the proceeding and the judgment was not against the manifest weight
 of the evidence.

¶2 Defendant-appellant Quinn Smith appeals from an order of eviction entered against her in

the circuit court of Cook County on June 6, 2025. For the reasons that follow, we affirm.

 BACKGROUND
 No. 1-25-1339

¶3 On November 16, 2023, plaintiff-appellee Quincy Smith, defendant’s twin brother, filed a

complaint for eviction against defendant, seeking possession only, of property located at 4940 S.

East End Avenue, #20, Chicago, Illinois. Attached as an exhibit to the complaint was a copy of

the 120-day notice of intent to evict, dated June 11, 2023, indicating that the tenancy would expire

on October 31, 2023. Additionally attached was plaintiff’s affidavit, wherein he averred that there

was “no current lease between the parties with respect to the premises.”

¶4 Notice to defendant of plaintiff’s complaint for eviction was ultimately achieved by posting

on January 29, 2024. Defendant entered her appearance on February 28, 2024. In what would be

defendant’s third motion to dismiss, filed March 28, 2024, she argued that she did not live at the

East End property and attached, as an exhibit, a property tax bill addressed to her for a Colfax

Avenue address in Chicago.

¶5 In his May 29, 2024, response to the motion to dismiss, plaintiff attached as an exhibit a

complaint for discrimination filed by defendant in the United States District Court for the Northern

District of Illinois, captioned “Quinn Smith v. Barclay Condominium Home Owners’

Association.” Relevant here, the federal court complaint alleged that plaintiff, Quinn Smith

(defendant here), is the owner of “a condominium unit at 4940 East End, Unit 20B in Chicago,

Illinois 60615.” The federal court complaint additionally alleged that “on or about 2023,” plaintiff

Quinn and her mother, Odessa Smith, moved into the condominium located on East End Avenue.

On July 2, 2024, the circuit court in this case denied defendant’s motion to dismiss.

¶6 On July 23, 2024, defendant filed her answer, affirmative defenses, and counterclaims

against plaintiff. Among the affirmative defenses, defendant asserted that plaintiff had “unclean

hands," she was not a “bona fide tenant,” and she was a co-owner of the East End property. On

July 31, 2024, plaintiff filed a motion to strike and dismiss defendant’s affirmative defenses and

 -2-
 No. 1-25-1339

counterclaims. Attached as an exhibit to plaintiff’s motion was a copy of a quitclaim deed,

recorded on February 6, 2018, and that identified plaintiff as the sole owner of the East End

property. On September 9, 2024, the circuit court granted plaintiff’s motion to strike and dismiss

defendant’s affirmative defenses and counterclaim.

¶7 On September 20, 2024, plaintiff filed an amended complaint in which he added as a

defendant “Odessa Smith, aka Odessa Norals.” We note, however, that Odessa Smith, who is

plaintiff’s and defendant’s mother, is not a party to this appeal. Defendant filed an answer,

affirmative defenses, asserting improper service, and counterclaims, alleging, inter alia, breach of

warranty of habitability and breach of contract regarding an alleged loan to plaintiff from Odessa

Smith and seeking a declaration on non-tenancy. Added as alternatives were claims for retaliatory

eviction, unjust enrichment, and violations of Chicago’s Residential Landlord and Tenant

Ordinance (“RLTO”). On May 5, 2025, with the exception of defendant’s claim for violation of

the RLTO, the trial court granted plaintiff’s motion to strike and deny defendant’s affirmative

defenses and counterclaims.

¶8 Following the close of discovery, the case proceeded to a bench trial that commenced on

May 29, 2025, and, by court order, continued on June 6, 2025. At the close of evidence, the trial

court entered an order for eviction. Although there is no transcript of the trial proceedings, included

in the record is a certified bystander’s report, dated December 5, 2025, and signed by the presiding

trial judge. See Ill. S. Ct. R. 323 (c) (eff. July 1, 2017).

¶9 Briefly, according to the bystander’s report, on May 29, 2025, immediately after the court

called the case, counsel for defendant stated that his client never lived at the subject property and

asserted to the court that it could grant plaintiff an eviction against the condo unit for all known or

 -3-
 No. 1-25-1339

unknown tenants. However, plaintiff objected. The court then permitted the parties an opportunity

to discuss settlement. No settlement agreement having been reached, the parties proceeded to trial.

¶ 10 Plaintiff first called as a witness Christopher Moore, a process server employed by “It’s

Your Serve.” After being sworn in by the trial judge, Moore testified that he served defendant a

120-day notice. He explained that he knocked on the door of the subject property, defendant

answered the door, and he handed her the 120-day notice. Moore identified defendant in court as

the person he had served. On cross-examination, Moore testified that when defendant answered

the door, he asked who she was, she identified herself, and he then handed her the notice.

¶ 11 Next up to testify was defendant. She stated that she lived at a property on Colfax Avenue

in Chicago that she owns with her mother. She never lived at the East End property, and she never

signed a lease agreement with plaintiff. Upon being shown a lease agreement (Exhibit A), she

stated that it was “a fraudulent lease,” on “metadata” and that the signature that appeared on the

document was not hers. Further, defendant stated that she never applied to the Illinois Rental

Assistance program and that she had never seen the application (Exhibit B). When shown a

cashier’s check for $2,400 made payable “to Quincy Smith for 2 payments of 1200” (Exhibit C),

she acknowledged that the memo on the check stated “Rent,” and that she had written the check

from her business account in order to receive a “write-off on [her] taxes.”

¶ 12 Plaintiff’s testimony essentially contradicted defendant’s testimony regarding the lease

agreement, the cashier’s check, and the rental assistance application. On cross-examination, he

testified that he and defendant applied for rental assistance because defendant wanted to pay him

back some rent payments. He additionally testified that defendant, to whom he had given his proxy

with the condominium homeowner’s association (“HOA”) and management company, was

 -4-
 No. 1-25-1339

“fraudulently telling the HOA and Management that she was the owner of the [ ] unit and causing

all kinds of problems with the building staff, management and HOA.”

¶ 13 Following plaintiff’s testimony, trial was recessed until June 6, 2025. Once trial resumed,

defendant was again called to testify. Her testimony was essentially the same as that given at the

May 29th proceeding.

¶ 14 At the close of the evidence, the trial court recalled the exhibits presented and then

recounted the testimony. The court stated that in light of defendant’s testimony that she “lied to

her bookkeeper to commit fraud on her tax returns,” it was hard to believe her testimony. The court

stated that all of the evidence indicated that defendant had a tenancy at the property and that the

lease had turned into a month-to-month tenancy. The trial judge additionally noted that defendant

admitted that she has “a key and fob and access to the subject property” which confirms that she

is in possession of the property. The court then granted the eviction.

¶ 15 On June 27, 2025, defendant filed a motion to vacate the court’s judgment for possession

to which she attached affidavits from herself and from her mother, Odessa Smith. Both affidavits

averred that defendant did not live at the East End property. On July 1, 2025, defendant filed a

motion to stay enforcement of the eviction order. On July 3, 2025, the court denied defendant’s

motion for stay, and on July 16, 2025, the court denied the motion to vacate the order of eviction.

¶ 16 Included in the record is a stipulation, signed by the parties and filed in the circuit court on

January 16, 2026, which states that the following trial exhibits, inter alia, “were approved in the

certified bystander’s report and were admitted during the proceedings:” “Exhibit A – Lease

Agreement between Quinn and Quincy,” “Exhibit B – Rental Assistance Program Application,”

“Exhibit C - $2400 rent Cashier’s Check,” and “Exhibit D – Text messages Quinn to Quincy.”

 -5-
 No. 1-25-1339

¶ 17 Defendant filed her notice of appeal on July 17, 2025. We have taken the appeal on

defendant’s opening brief and the record only. See First Capitol Mortgage Corp. v. Talandis

Construction Corp., 63 Ill. 2d 128, 133 (1976) (the reviewing court may take a case on appellant’s

brief only). For the reasons that follow, we affirm.

 ANALYSIS

¶ 18 Here on appeal, defendant essentially contends that there was no trial as there was no

competent evidence presented to support the court’s judgments. In that regard she argues that no

witnesses were sworn in prior to offering testimony, the lease was not admitted into evidence, and

plaintiff failed to mark or offer any exhibits into evidence. Next, and seemingly her strongest

contention, defendant argues that plaintiff failed to prove the “essential elements necessary to

obtain an order of possession.”

¶ 19 We begin our analysis with a review of defendant’s challenges to procedural errors alleged

to have occurred during the “trial.” With respect to defendant’s argument that no witnesses were

sworn in, we note that the bystander’s report indicates that Moore was sworn in by the court. The

report does not indicate, however, whether the other witnesses, that included plaintiff and

defendant, were also sworn.

¶ 20 It is conceivable to us that the bystander’s report, unlike a transcript of proceedings, does

not reflect verbatim all that was said or done during the proceeding. That said, we also note that

the report does not indicate that any objection was made regarding the court’s alleged failure to

administer oaths to each witness. Thus, we deem any irregularity regarding the administering of

oaths to have been forfeited. Calabrese v. Benitez, 2015 IL App (3d) 130827, ¶ 17 (failure to voice

an objection and to raise the issue in a post-trial motion forfeits the issue on appeal); see 81 Am.

Jur. 2d Witnesses § 633 (August 2026 Update) (“any irregularity in failing to swear a witness is

 -6-
 No. 1-25-1339

waived where the witness is permitted to testify without an objection being interposed”); id. § 634

(although the administration of the oath to a witness is fundamental, absent a timely objection,

unsworn testimony is not a nullity).

¶ 21 Although some authorities state that the failure to swear a witness cannot be dismissed as

a mere irregularity (id. § 633 (August 2026 Update)), our research has found no Illinois case that

so prov

COURT OF APPEALS OF VIRGINIA 
Record No. 0523-25-3 
BRUCE A. BUREN, ET AL. 
v. 
LAKEVIEW LOAN SERVICING, LLC 
Present: Judges Causey, Raphael and Duffan 
Argued at Lexington, Virginia 
Opinion Issued October 13, 2026* 
FROM THE CIRCUIT COURT OF ROCKBRIDGE COUNTY 
Christopher B. Russell, Judge 
James V. Doss, III, for appellants. 
Ronald J. Guillot, Jr. (Samuel I. White, P.C., on brief), for appellee. 
MEMORANDUM OPINION BY 
JUDGE DORIS HENDERSON CAUSEY 
 Bruce and Maria Buren appeal the circuit court’s order granting Lakeview Loan 
Servicing, LLC summary judgment in their dispute over possession of a foreclosed home. The 
Burens contend that the circuit court lacked subject matter jurisdiction to grant summary 
judgment. We disagree and affirm the circuit court. 

* This opinion is not designated for publication. See Code § 17.1-413(A). 
 - 2 - 
BACKGROUND1 
In 2018, the Burens purchased three parcels of land and a home in Rockbridge County. 
They partially financed the purchase with a $367,860 loan guaranteed by the Government National 
Mortgage Association and secured by a Veterans Administration deed of trust. The Administration 
assigned the security instrument to Lakeview, the loan servicer. Following a foreclosure sale in 
October 2022, a trustee’s deed transferred ownership of the home to Lakeview. Lakeview then 
transferred title to the Administration in April 2023, who reconveyed ownership back to Lakeview 
by a quitclaim deed in October 2023. 
In September 2023, the Burens sued Lakeview, the substitute trustee, and the 
Administration; they served only Lakeview with their complaint. They challenged Lakeview’s title, 
claiming that Lakeview had agreed to a forbearance of their loan payments. According to the 
Burens, the forbearance agreement deferred their missed payments to the end of the loan, allowing 
them to resume payments at the end of the COVID-19 pandemic. They also claimed that they had 
not received notice of the foreclosure sale and that the trustee’s deed only assessed the value of one 
of the three parcels. For these reasons, they claimed the foreclosure sale was void. In the fall of 
2024, the circuit court sustained Lakeview’s demurrer and dismissed the suit against Lakeview with 
prejudice. The lawsuit remained pending against the unserved defendants. 
In October 2024, Lakeview sought possession of the home and provided the Burens with a 
three-day notice to vacate. After the notice expired, the Burens continued to possess the home. 
Lakeview then filed an unlawful detainer action in the General District Court (GDC) of Rockbridge 

1 “Under well-settled principles, we review the record applying the same standard a trial 
court must adopt in reviewing a motion for summary judgment, accepting as true those 
inferences from the facts that are most favorable to the [Burens], unless the inferences are forced, 
strained, or contrary to reason.” Neal v. Sec’y of the Dep’t of Veterans Affairs, 79 Va. App. 1, 
3-4 (2023) (quoting Fultz v. Delhaize Am., Inc., 278 Va. 84, 88 (2009)). 
 - 3 - 
County. The GDC entered judgment for Lakeview, awarding it possession of the property. The 
Burens timely appealed to the circuit court. 
In circuit court, Lakeview moved for summary judgment. Lakeview argued that it had a 
right to possession, as shown by the duly recorded quitclaim deed, its dismissal from the Burens’ 
lawsuit, and the notice to vacate. Lakeview also argued that the Burens had not responded to 
Lakeview’s requests for admissions nor objected to Lakeview’s exhibits. The Burens argued that 
the circuit court lacked jurisdiction to grant summary judgment because their suit challenging title 
remained pending against the unserved defendants. The circuit court granted summary judgment to 
Lakeview, awarding it possession of the property. The Burens appeal. 
ANALYSIS 
Subject matter jurisdiction “is a question of law we review de novo.” Parrish v. Fannie 
Mae, 292 Va. 44, 49 (2016) (quoting Glasser & Glasser, PLC v. Jack Bays, Inc., 285 Va. 358, 
369 (2013)). General district courts have statutory authority to try actions for unlawful detainer, 
but they have no authority to try issues of title. Id. at 50. “[W]hen exercising its appellate 
jurisdiction in a de novo appeal, the circuit court’s subject matter jurisdiction is derivative of the 
court not of record from which that appeal is taken.” Id. at 49. Thus, a circuit court also has no 
authority to resolve issues of title in an unlawful detainer action appealed from general district 
court. Id. 
Yet issues of title may arise in unlawful detainer actions. “An unlawful detainer is an 
action brought against ‘a defendant who lawfully entered into possession of real property but 
whose right to lawful possession has since expired.’” Neal v. Sec’y of the Dep’t of Veterans 
Affairs, 79 Va. App. 1, 5-6 (2023) (quoting Parrish, 292 Va. at 50). The out-of-possession 
plaintiff must show that he “has a superior right of possession to the defendant.” Id. at 6. When 
the unlawful detainer is based on a foreclosure sale, the plaintiff’s right of possession is acquired 
 - 4 - 
after the defendant’s entry and is “derivative of the title received at the foreclosure sale.” 
Id. at 6, 8. Generally, a foreclosure-purchaser plaintiff establishes a right of possession by 
producing a trustee’s deed. Id. at 6. But as the Supreme Court explained in Parrish, a defendant 
alleging sufficient facts challenging the validity of the trustee’s deed may rebut the plaintiff’s 
prima facie case for possession. 292 Va. at 51 n.2. In that situation, the “general district court’s 
lack of subject matter jurisdiction to try title supersedes its subject matter jurisdiction to try 
unlawful detainer[,] and the court must dismiss the case without prejudice.” Id. at 52. 
Even so, not “any naked allegation” of invalidity places “the deed in doubt, thereby 
divesting the general district court of jurisdiction.” Id. The allegation must be legitimate. Id. 
To be legitimate, “the allegations must be sufficient to survive a demurrer had the homeowner 
filed a complaint in circuit court seeking such relief.” Id. The general district court may assess 
whether the defendant has made a legitimate allegation. Id. at 51 n.2. If the allegations are 
insufficient, then subject matter jurisdiction is retained, and the unlawful detainer case may be 
resolved on the merits. Id. at 53. 
The Burens contend that Lakeview was not entitled to summary judgment because the 
circuit court lacked subject matter jurisdiction to adjudicate the unlawful detainer while their lawsuit 
challenging title remained pending.2 However, the Burens’ argument to this effect is merely 
conclusory. “We have many times pointed out that on appeal the judgment of the lower court is 
presumed to be correct and the burden is on the appellant to present to us a sufficient record from 

2 In a separate assignment of error, the Burens assert that the taking of their private 
property violated due process. An opening brief must contain “[t]he standard of review and the 
argument (including principles of law and authorities) relating to each assignment of error.” 
Rule 5A:20(e). “Unsupported assertions of error ‘do not merit appellate consideration.’” 
Bartley v. Commonwealth, 67 Va. App. 740, 744 (2017) (quoting Jones v. Commonwealth, 51 
Va. App. 730, 734 (2008)). The Burens provided no argument on brief to support the due 
process claim, and we find that failure significant. Jay v. Commonwealth, 275 Va. 510, 520 
(2008). As a result, the due process argument is waived, and we limit our analysis to the 
jurisdictional question. Winters v. Winters, 73 Va. App. 581, 597 (2021). 
 - 5 - 
which we can determine whether the lower court has erred in the respect complained of.” Bon 
Secours-DePaul Med. Ctr., Inc. v. Rogakos-Russell, 304 Va. 1, 16 n.7 (2025) (quoting Justis v. 
Young, 202 Va. 631, 632 (1961)). Relatedly, under Rule 5A:20(e), “[t]he opening brief of 
appellant must contain . . . [t]he standard of review and the argument (including principles of law 
and authorities) relating to each assignment of error.” 
Here, the Burens provide no argument and cite no cases or principles of law that explain or 
bear on the potential relevance of Parrish on a simultaneously pending suit for declaratory 
judgment against unserved parties. The brief merely asserts that Parrish “still controls here” 
because the appellants’ “complaint for declaratory judgment [has not] been dismissed as to all 
defendants.” But they provide no explanation for why the fact that this complaint remains pending 
against some defendants means that allegations contesting the trustee’s deed “sufficient to survive a 
demurrer” have been made. Parrish, 292 Va. at 52. It is not clear from the Burens’ argument why 
these particular, unserved complaints should be regarded as “sufficient to survive a demurrer.” Id. 
And the Burens make no argument—making the point impossible to reach on this appeal—that 
would elucidate the potential significance of any unserved complaint under the Parrish standard. 
The Burens, bearing the burden of establishing error on appeal, have not provided this Court 
with sufficient argument to persuade us that the trial court erred in holding that the general rule in 
Parrish controlled. They have not shown that the trial court was wrong in holding that they failed 
to make allegations contesting the trustee’s deed that are “sufficient to survive a demurrer.” 
Parrish, 292 Va. at 52. See Bon Secours-DePaul Med. Ctr., 304 Va. at 16 n.7 (noting the 
appellant bears the burden of showing both where in the record and how the lower court erred). 
Therefore, we will affirm the judgment of the circuit court. 
 - 6 - 
CONCLUSION 
The appellants have shown no error in the circuit court’s exercise of jurisdiction over the 
unlawful detainer action. We affirm the circuit court’s award of summary judgment to 
Lakeview. 
Affirmed.

COURT OF APPEALS OF VIRGINIA 
Record No. 0657-25-1 
RECYCLED PROPERTIES, LLC 
v. 
THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF CHESAPEAKE, ET AL. 
Present: Judges Beales, White and Duffan 
Argued at Norfolk, Virginia 
Opinion Issued October 13, 2026* 
FROM THE CIRCUIT COURT OF THE CITY OF CHESAPEAKE 
David J. Whitted, Judge 
Joseph V. Sherman (J. Bryan Plumlee; Lauren C. Rose; Nicole K. Pasho; Poole Brooke Plumlee 
PC, on briefs), for appellant. 
Ellen F. Bergren, Chief Deputy City Attorney (Catherine H. Lindley, City Attorney; Jessica R. 
Turner, Assistant City Attorney, on brief), for appellees. 
MEMORANDUM OPINION BY 
JUDGE KEVIN M. DUFFAN 
Recycled Properties, LLC appeals the circuit court’s order sustaining the City Council of the 
City of Chesapeake’s, the City of Chesapeake’s, and Jay Tate’s (the Director of Development and 
Permits) (collectively, “the City”) demurrer to its complaint challenging the City’s disapproval of its 
proposed site plan. On appeal, Recycled Properties argues that the circuit court erroneously 
sustained the City’s demurrer. We disagree, and affirm the circuit court. 
BACKGROUND 
Recycled Properties operates a construction and demolition debris landfill and borrow pit 
in Chesapeake, Virginia. The property’s operations are legally nonconforming. In May 2024, 

* This opinion is not designated for publication. See Code § 17.1-413(A). 
 - 2 - 
Recycled Properties submitted a site plan to the City’s Department of Development and Permits 
to construct a warehouse and office building (collectively, “the buildings”) on the property. In 
August 2024, the City disapproved the site plan. Grounds for disapproval were that: first, the 
buildings depicted in the site plan were an expansion to the legal nonconforming use existing on 
the property, in violation of Chesapeake Zoning Ordinance (CZO) § 15-104(A)(3); second, 
approval of the site plan would not be granted until further information on the buildings’ use was 
provided; and third, a conditional use permit must be obtained for the lawfully nonconforming 
operations as a condition to approving the site plan. 
After the City denied the site plan, Recycled Properties timely appealed under Code 
§ 15.2-2260(E) and CZO § 18-303(B), and it attached the disapproval letter to its complaint. It 
first argued that the site plan’s disapproval was not properly based on applicable ordinances and 
was arbitrary and capricious.1 Second, it argued that conditioning the site plan’s approval on 
obtaining a conditional use permit for the entire lawfully nonconforming operations was an 
unconstitutional condition. 
The City demurred. The City contended that the CZO authorized the denial and that 
Recycled Properties had failed to show that the new building would not expand the 
nonconforming use or require additional information. The City also argued that Recycled 
Properties failed to plead any legally sufficient unconstitutional condition. Recycled Properties 
opposed the demurrer, arguing that the CZO did not require it to prove that the site plan is not an 
expansion of a lawfully nonconforming use or to provide “adequate information” about the 
proposed building. It also sought damages under Code § 15.2-2208.1, arguing that the City 

1 The allegations of arbitrary and capricious conduct were focused on the notices of past 
zoning violations, which the City withdrew as a ground for denial of the site plan. 
 - 3 - 
unlawfully conditioned approval of the site plan on obtaining a conditional use permit for 
existing operations. 
At the hearing on the demurrer, the City grounded its denial on the unlawful expansion of 
a nonconforming use and withdrew the preexisting zoning violations from part of its denial. 
According to the City, the “sole meaningful issue” was a lack of “adequate information received 
on whether the building[s were] an expansion of the legal nonconformity.” On this issue, 
Recycled Properties argued that the City would “never accept the information [it would have] 
provided” and that nothing in the CZO authorized the City to “require adequate information.” 
Recycled Properties also contended that the evidence would show there was no expansion of the 
nonconforming use and that it had a vested right to add buildings in support of its lawfully 
nonconforming use. Its position was that to survive demurrer, it only had to allege that the 
denial was arbitrary, capricious, and failed to accord with zoning ordinances. 
After the hearing, the circuit court sustained the demurrer. The court found that based on 
the allegations and attachments, the City had authority to deny the site plan, and that the “City’s 
action at this point was proper.” The court held that Recycled Properties “failed to adequately 
plead its appeal on the requirement to submit additional information on the potential illegal 
expansion of a legal nonconformity.” The circuit court ruled that Recycled Properties “may file 
a new site plan application.” Recycled Properties appeals. 
ANALYSIS 
“A trial court’s decision sustaining a demurrer presents a question of law which we review 
de novo.” Squire v. Va. Hous. Dev. Auth., 287 Va. 507, 514 (2014) (quoting Harris v. Kreutzer, 
271 Va. 188, 196 (2006)). “In reviewing a trial court’s order sustaining a demurrer, ‘we are 
required to address the same issue that the trial court addressed, namely whether the [complaint] 
alleged sufficient facts to constitute a foundation in law for the judgment sought.’” Eagle Harbor 
 - 4 - 
L.L.C. v. Isle of Wight County, 271 Va. 603, 611 (2006) (quoting Hubbard v. Dresser, Inc., 271 Va. 
117, 119 (2006)). “The purpose of a demurrer is to determine whether the pleading and any proper 
attachments state a cause of action upon which relief can be given.” Steward v. Holland Family 
Props., LLC, 284 Va. 282, 286 (2012). In reviewing a demurrer, all factual allegations pleaded in 
the complaint are treated as true; but the reviewing court need not “accept the veracity of 
conclusions of law camouflaged as factual allegations or inferences.” Coward v. Wellmont Health 
Sys., 295 Va. 351, 359 (2018) (quoting AGCS Marine Ins. v. Arlington Cnty., 293 Va. 469, 473 
(2017)). 
A trial court must sustain a planning commission’s decision approving or disapproving a 
plat unless the decision “was not properly based on the ordinance applicable thereto, or was 
arbitrary or capricious.” James v. City of Falls Church, 280 Va. 31, 41 (2010) (quoting Code 
§§ 15.2-2259(D), -2260(E)). The Supreme Court of Virginia has defined “arbitrary and capricious” 
as an act that is “willful,” “unreasonable,” and “taken ‘without consideration or in disregard of facts 
or law.’” Id. at 42 (quoting Sch. Bd. of the City of Norfolk v. Wescott, 254 Va. 218, 224 (1997)). 
“On appeal, ‘the trial court’s judgment is presumed correct and will not be set aside unless the 
judgment is plainly wrong or unsupported by the evidence.’” Id. at 41 (quoting Bd. of Supervisors 
v. Greengael, L.L.C., 271 Va. 266, 277 (2006)). 
Localities may require submission of site plans for review. See Code § 15.2-2260 and Code 
§ 15.2-2259 (authorizing a designated agent to act on any proposed plat); Code § 15.2-2286(A)(8) 
(providing that a zoning ordinance may require “submission and approval of a plan of development 
prior to the issuance of building permits to assure compliance with regulations contained in such 
zoning ordinance”). The locality reviews the site plans for compliance with existing plans, 
ordinances, and standards identified in CZO § 18-204. If the locality denies the plan, it must 
identify reasons for disapproval and corrections that could permit approval. Code § 15.2-2259(A); 
 - 5 - 
Code § 15.2-2260(C). If a locality’s “designated agent disapproves a plat and the applicant 
contends that the disapproval was not properly based on the ordinance applicable thereto, or was 
arbitrary or capricious, he may appeal to the circuit court having jurisdiction” of such land. Code 
§ 15.2-2259(D); Code § 15.2-2260(E). 
I. There were no facts pled that the City’s denial of the site plan was arbitrary, capricious, or 
outside applicable ordinance provisions. 
Recycled Properties argues that the circuit court erred by sustaining the City’s demurrer 
because it sufficiently pled that the site plan disapproval was not based on the applicable ordinance 
and that it was arbitrary or capricious. We disagree. 
In its complaint, Recycled Properties stated that the disapproval of the site plan was 
erroneous because the CZO does not require applicants to: (1) prove that projects are not expansions 
or additional structures supporting a lawfully nonconforming use, (2) provide “adequate 
information” explaining the use of the site plan, and (3) obtain a conditional use permit to expand 
the existing lawfully nonconforming operation.2 

2 In the introduction of its opening brief, Recycled Properties claims that the circuit 
court’s denial of its site plan was “unconstitutional.” Its constitutional argument is not included 
in an assignment of error and is not argued otherwise in the opening brief. According to Rule 
5A:20(e), the opening brief must contain “the argument (including principles of law and 
authorities) relating to each assignment of error.” The effect of this omission is waiver. Bartley 
v. Commonwealth, 67 Va. App. 740, 744 (2017) (“Unsupported assertions of error ‘do not merit 
appellate consideration.’” (quoting Jones v. Commonwealth, 51 Va. App. 730, 734 (2008))). For 
that reason, we do not reach Recycled Property’s constitutional argument. We do note that this 
argument was raised in Count II of Recycled Property’s complaint, but that has no bearing on the 
present determination by this Court on appeal because Rule 5A:20(e) applies to briefing in this 
Court—not to briefing that occurred in the trial court. 
 - 6 - 
However, Recycled Properties also attached the City’s denial letter, which cited CZO 
§ 15-104(A)(3)3 and § 18-302(A),4 authorizing the denial of a site plan where a proposed building 
would alter or expand a nonconforming use or where more information would be necessary to 
evaluate conformity. Bd. of Supervisors v. Cohn, 296 Va. 465 (2018) (holding that a locality may 
preclude the expansion of a nonconforming use under Code § 15.2-2307(C)). The denial letter 
stated that approval would not be granted until Recycled Properties provided more information on 
the proposed building’s use and obtained a conditional use permit to support expanding the 
nonconforming use. 
The denial letter refutes Recycled Properties’s legal conclusions “camouflaged as factual 
allegations or inferences.” Coward, 295 Va. at 359. No allegations in its complaint refute the 
factual and legal grounds asserted in the letter—that the proposed building would alter or expand 
the nonconforming use and more information would be needed to evaluate the expansion. 
Consequently, the circuit court was correct in determining that Recycled Properties had not 
sufficiently pled facts supporting its legal conclusion that the denial was arbitrary, capricious, or 
outside ordinance provisions. Accordingly, we find no error in the court’s ruling. 
II. The circuit court did not convert the demurrer to summary judgment. 
 Last, Recycled Properties argues that the circuit court erred because it ruled on the merits 
of Recycled Properties’s complaint on a summary judgment standard instead of the proper 
demurrer standard. We disagree.

IN THE COMMONWEALTH COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA 

Carl Edward Meyer, Jr. and : 
CASRR Meyer Business Trust, : 
 Petitioners : 
 : 
 v. : No. 625 F.R. 2022 
 : ARGUED: September 14, 2026 
Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, : 
 Respondent : 

BEFORE: HONORABLE CHRISTINE FIZZANO CANNON, Judge 
HONORABLE LORI A. DUMAS, Judge 
 HONORABLE BONNIE BRIGANCE LEADBETTER, Senior Judge 

OPINION NOT REPORTED 

MEMORANDUM OPINION BY 
SENIOR JUDGE LEADBETTER FILED: October 13, 2026 

 Taxpayers, Carl Edward Meyer, Jr. and the CASRR Meyer Business 
Trust (hereafter simply CASRR Trust), petition for review of the order of the Board 
of Finance and Revenue (Board) sustaining a decision of the Board of Appeals 
(BOA), upholding the imposition of realty transfer tax on a deed conveying real 
estate from Meyer to the CASRR Trust. For the following reasons, we affirm. 
Factual and Procedural Background 
 The pertinent facts are not in dispute, having been established by joint 
stipulation of the parties.1 Meyer is an attorney licensed to practice law in both Ohio 

1 The Board does not certify a record to this Court. Pa.R.A.P. 1571(f). Rather, as 
factfinder, we review “decisions of the Board de novo based on stipulated facts or a record created 
before this Court,” or a combination thereof. Synthes USA HQ, Inc. v. Commonwealth, 236 A.3d 
1190, 1193 n.4 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2020), aff’d, 289 A.3d 846 (Pa. 2023) [citing Pa.R.A.P. 1571(h); 
Plum Borough Sch. Dist. v. Commonwealth, 860 A.2d 1155 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2004)]. Here, the parties 
(Footnote continued on next page…) 
2 
and Pennsylvania. Stipulation of Facts (SOF) ¶ 4. In December 2019, Meyer and 
his wife, Arshia H. Meyer (Mrs. Meyer), established both the CASRR Trust and the 
Meyer Family Revocable Trust (Family Trust) under Ohio law. SOF ¶¶ 5-7. Meyer 
and his wife are the settlors and trustees of the CASRR Trust , and all shares of the 
CASRR Trust are owned by the Family Trust. SOF ¶¶ 9, 12. 
 At the heart of this matter are two transactions conveying the deed to 
property located at 100 Grayhawk Way South, Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania 
(Property). In March 2020, NVR, Inc. executed a deed conveying the Property to 
Meyer, and since that time the Meyers have used the Property as their personal 
residence. SOF ¶¶ 16-17; SOF, Ex. B. Upon the recording of this deed, Meyer paid 
$9,647.45 in fees and taxes, including realty transfer tax . SOF ¶ 17 ; SOF, Ex. B . 
Then in August 2020, Meyer executed a deed conveying the Property to the CASRR 
Trust. SOF ¶ 18; SOF, Ex. C. That same day, Meyer executed and recorded a Realty 
Transfer Tax Statement of Value reporting the assessed and computed values for the 
Property, and claiming an exemption from realty transfer tax because the Property 
was transferred to a trust. SOF ¶ 20; SOF, Ex. C. 
 In December 2021, the Department of Revenue issued notices of 
assessment to Taxpayers imposing realty transfer tax in the amount of $9,797.96, 
plus interest and fees, for the conveyance of the Property from Meyer to the CASRR 
Trust. SOF ¶ 21; SOF, Exs. D, E . Taxpayers timely petitioned BOA for 
reassessment as to this second conveyance. SOF ¶ 22; SOF, Ex. F. BOA issued a 
single decision and order sustaining the Department’s assessments and Taxpayers 

filed a stipulation of facts (SOF) on Ju ne 9, 2025. While these “[s]tipulations of fact are binding 
upon both the parties and th e Court,” we may draw our own legal conclusions. Ebersole v. 
Commonwealth, 303 A.3d 546, 550 n.5 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2023) (quotation omitted). 

3 
subsequently filed a petition for review with the Board. SOF ¶¶ 25-26; SOF, Exs. 
H-J. Following argument, the Board issued a decision and order sustaining the 
assessments in their entirety, and Taxpayers then petitioned this Court for review. 
SOF ¶¶ 28-29; SOF, Exs. L-M. 
Issues 
 Taxpayers assert multiple issues in their brief to this Court , which we 
paraphrase as follows: (1) whether the conveyance of the Property from Meyer to 
the CASRR Trust is exempt from realty transfer tax because the CASRR Trust is a 
living trust and not a business trust; (2) whether Taxpayers proved that Meyer was 
acting as an agent or straw party and therefore they are entitled to the principal/agent 
exemption to the realty transfer tax; and (3) whether Taxpayers should have been 
granted leave to file a corrective or voided deed to negate realty transfer tax on the 
second conveyance.2 
Discussion 
 Before turning to the merits, we briefly review the statutory provisions 
at issue. Section 1102-C of the Tax Reform Code of 19713 (Code) generally imposes 
a realty transfer tax on all real estate title transfers. Ebersole v. Commonwealth, 303 
A.3d 546, 553 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2023) . However, certain transfers are specifically 
excluded from the tax, including: 

2 Taxpayers also argue that the Board “committed a clear error of law and abused its 
discretion by allowing the D[epartment]’s legal counsel of record [] . . . to engage in the 
unauthorized practice of law [,]” despite the fact that Counsel for the Department is admitted to 
practice law in the Commonwealth, and is in good s tanding. Taxpayers’ Br. at 24. After the 
Commonwealth’s attempts to amicably resolve this issue failed, it filed an application to strike the 
portions of Taxpayers’ brief pertaining to the purported unauthorized practice argument. Rather 
than muddy the waters of this tax appeal with an unfounded and lamentable claim, we addressed 
the issue in a separate Memorandum and Order filed September 22, 2026. 
3 Act of March 4, 1971, P.L. 6, as amended, added by the Act of May 5, 1981, P.L. 36, 72 
P.S. § 8102-C. 
4 

(4) A transfer for no or nominal actual consideration which 
corrects or confirms a transfer previously recorded, but 
which does not extend or limit existing record legal title or 
interest. 

. . . . 

(8) A transfer for no or nominal actual consideration to a 
trustee of an ordinary trust where the transfer of the same 
property would be exempt if the transfer was made directly 
from the grantor to all of the possible beneficiaries that are 
entitled to receive the property or proceeds from the sale 
of the property under the trust, whether or not such 
beneficiaries are contingent or specifically named. A trust 
clause which identifies the contingent beneficiaries by 
reference to the heirs of the trust settlor as determined by 
the laws of the intestate succession shall not disqualify a 
transfer from the exclusion provided by this clause. No 
such exemption shall be granted unless the recorder of 
deeds is presented with a copy of the trust instrument that 
clearly identifies the grantor and all possible beneficiaries. 

(8.1) A transfer for no or nominal consideration to a trustee 
of a living trust from the settlor of the living trust. No such 
exemption shall be granted unless the recorder of deeds is 
presented with a copy of the living trust instrument. 

. . . . 

(11) A transfer: 

 (i) for no or nominal actual consideration between 
principal and agent or straw party[.] 

Section 1102-C.3 of the Code, added by the Act of July 2, 1986, P.L. 318, 72 P.S. § 
8102-C.3. The Code defines the terms “living trust” and “ordinary trust” as follows: 

“Living trust.” Any trust, other than a business trust , 
intended as a will substitute by the settlor which becomes 
effective during the lifetime of the settlor, but from which 
5 
trust distributions cannot be made to any beneficiaries 
other than the settlor prior to the death of the settlor. 

. . . . 

“Ordinary trust.” Any trust, other than a business trust or 
a living trust, which takes effect during the lifetime of the 
settlor and for which the trustees of the trust take title to 
property primarily for the purpose of protecting, managing 
or conserving it until distribution to the named 
beneficiaries of the trust. An ordinary trust does not 
include a trust that has an objective to carry on business 
and divide gains, nor does it either expressly or impliedly 
have any of the following features: the treatment of 
beneficiaries as associates, the treatment of the interests in 
the trust as personal property, the f ree transferability of 
beneficial interests in the trust, centralized management by 
the trustee or the beneficiaries, or continuity of life. 

Section 1101-C of the Code, 72 P.S. § 8101-C (emphasis added).4 
 Taxpayers maintain that the CASRR Trust – despite its name and the 
express language of the deed of trust creating it – is a living trust rather than a 
business trust; therefore, the deed transferring title to the Property from Meyer to the 
CASRR Trust is exempt from realty transfer tax under Section 1102-C.3(8.1) of the 
Code. Both the CASRR Trust and the Family Trust were created pursuant to Ohio 
law and, according to Taxpayers, they must “be governed, construed, interpreted, 
and administered in accordance with Ohio law.” Taxpayers’ Br. at 22. Along this 
line of reasoning, Taxpayers submit that title to property cannot be held in the name 
of a living trust under Ohio law, thus Meyer followed the industry practice in Ohio 
of establishing a “business trust,” i.e. the CASRR Trust, simply to hold title to the 
Property. In finding that the CASRR Trust was a business trust, the Board 

4 To be clear, Taxpayers do not claim that the CASRR Trust is an ordinary trust. However, 
the Code’s definition of the term is relevant as it delineates the features of a business trust for 
realty transfer tax purposes. 
6 
erroneously focused on the form rather than the substance of the transfer. Taxpayers 
further argue that the facts here are similar to those in Exton Plaza Associates v. 
Commonwealth, 763 A.2d 521 (Pa. Cmwlth. 1998) (Exton Plaza ), because the 
CASRR Trust is merely an extension of the Family Trust, which is a living trust, and 
because there was no actual change in interest or ownership when the Property was 
conveyed from Meyer to the CASRR Trust. 
 Taxpayers’ arguments pertaining to the nature of the CASRR Trust fail 
for multiple reasons. First and foremost, the Department’s assessments pertain to 
property located in the Commonwealth, the transfer of which was found to be taxable 
under the statutes of the Commonwealth by a n agency of the Commonwealth. 
Simply put, Ohio law is not at issue despite the fact that the CASRR Trust was 
organized under Ohio law. See, e.g., Section 1102-C of the Code, 72 P.S. § 8102-C 
(imposing realty transfer tax on documents transferring real estate “within this 
Commonwealth,” such as the Property here). 
 Next, regardless of Taxpayers’ purported intent, we agree with the 
Board’s conclusion that the CASRR Trust is a business trust. The Code explicitly 
excludes a business trust from the definition of either a living trust or an ordinary 
trust. See Section 1101-C of the Code, 72 P.S. § 8101 -C. Instead, business trusts 
are considered corporate entities under the Code, as its definition of “corporation” 
for realty transfer tax purposes includes business trusts “organized under the laws of 
this Commonwealth, the United States, or any other state , territory, or foreign 
country, or dependency. ” Id. (emphasis added) . “Corporations . . . are entities 
separate from their members, partners, stockholders or shareholders[,]” and unless 
otherwise excluded, documents transferring “title to real estate between . . . 
7 
corporations and the members, partners, shareholders or stockholders thereof are 
fully taxable.” Section 1102-C.4 of the Code, 72 P.S. § 8102-C.4. 
 Here, the parties stipulated that the CASRR Trust was expressly created 
under the laws of Ohio relating to business trusts. SOF ¶ 7 (citing Chapter 1746 of 
the Ohio Rev . Code Ann. §§ 1746.01-1746.99). But beyond its name and how it 
was established, the CASRR Trust bears the hallmarks of a business trust as provided 
under the Code’s realty transfer tax provisions. Most notably, the deed establishing
